Never, on any timescale that matters. The premise is a myth: window glass is an amorphous solid, and at room temperature its viscosity is so high that estimated relaxation times run far longer than the age of the universe. Calculations for ordinary soda-lime glass put noticeable flow at something like 10^20+ years, and medieval glass has shown no measurable sag in that time.

The thick-bottom effect in old windows comes from how the glass was made. Crown glass was spun into a disc, which left it uneven in thickness, and glaziers often installed the heavier edge down for stability. Cylinder glass, also common, had its own thickness variations. Some old panes are even installed with the thick edge on the side or top. Other evidence against flow: ancient glass lenses and Roman-era artifacts keep their shapes, and old telescope mirrors and optics haven't deformed.

Your house windows are float glass, which is flat to within very tight tolerances. They'll stay that way.
